name: Apabhraṃśa
confidence_why: Apabhraṃśa is an extinct literary stage whose accent was never written, and the authorities who inferred it from spelling and morphology disagree on the very type of system: Jacobi 1921 posits a Latin-like quantity accent competing with a stem-syllable accent, Pischel 1900 the inherited Vedic accent position, Tagare 1948 an accent on the initial syllable, and Bloch 1965 finds no decisive evidence for any regular word stress.

catalog_quote: Während im Prākrit die Stelle des Wortakzentes von der Prosodie des Wortes, einem mechanischen Prinzip, bestimmt gewesen zu sein scheint wie im Lateinischen, glaube ich beim Apabhraṃśa außerdem noch ein anderes und zwar organisches Prinzip annehmen zu sollen, das auch im Guzeratī wirksam ist. Dort trägt nämlich die Stammsilbe einen Akzent, der mit dem durch die Quantität bestimmten in Konkurrenz treten kann. Im Apabhraṃśa würde sich die Sache folgendermaßen darstellen. Das Verbum paṇāvai wäre auf der Stammsilbe betont, aber das Part. praes. paṇavānta hätte nach dem mechanischen Prinzip noch einen Nebenton auf der vorletzten Silbe haben müssen. Man darf annehmen, daß die Sprache bestrebt sein wird, solche doppelte Betonung nach Möglichkeit zu vereinfachen oder auszugleichen. Im Apabhraṃśa läßt sich dieses Streben deutlich erkennen bei zweisilbigen Endungen, indem nämlich diejenigen mit kurzer Pänultima entschieden denen mit langer und darum nebentoniger vorgezogen werden.

new_statements.quote: Während im Prākrit die Stelle des Wortakzentes von der Prosodie des Wortes, einem mechanischen Prinzip, bestimmt gewesen zu sein scheint wie im Lateinischen, glaube ich beim Apabhraṃśa außerdem noch ein anderes und zwar organisches Prinzip annehmen zu sollen, das auch im Guzeratī wirksam ist. Dort trägt nämlich die Stammsilbe einen Akzent, der mit dem durch die Quantität bestimmten in Konkurrenz treten kann. Im Apabhraṃśa würde sich die Sache folgendermaßen darstellen. Das Verbum paṇāvai wäre auf der Stammsilbe betont, aber das Part. praes. paṇavānta hätte nach dem mechanischen Prinzip noch einen Nebenton auf der vorletzten Silbe haben müssen.
new_statements.translation: Whereas in Prakrit the place of the word accent seems to have been determined by the prosody of the word, a mechanical principle, as in Latin, I believe that for Apabhramsa one must in addition assume another, organic principle, which is also at work in Gujarati. There, namely, the stem syllable carries an accent which can compete with the one determined by quantity. In Apabhramsa the matter would look as follows: the verb panāvai would be accented on the stem syllable, but the present participle panavānta would, by the mechanical principle, still have had a secondary accent on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jacobi: an expiratory accent whose place is fixed Latin-style by syllable weight (heavy penult, else further back), plus in Apabhramsa a competing accent on the verbal/nominal stem (root) syllable; the language tends to resolve the clash by preferring endings with a light penult. This is an inference from ending statistics, shortenings and geminations in a dead literary language, and it is contradicted by Pischel 1900 sec. 46 (poetic Apabhramsa keeps the Vedic, lexically free accent place), by Tagare 1948 (accent on the initial syllable; penult 'definitely unaccented' in Eastern Apabhramsa) and by Bloch 1934/1965 (no stress accent demonstrable for Middle Indian; the facts reflect quantitative rhythm).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jacobi: a quantity-determined 'Nebenton' (secondary accent) on a heavy penult can co-occur with the stem-syllable accent (panavānta); enclitics (vi, va, ji, ciya) throw an accent onto the final syllable of the preceding word (sec. 10, p. 8). Chatterji 1926 p. 276, reporting Jacobi 1893, adds a secondary stress on the first syllable for MIA generally.
new_statements.exceptions: Verse-final (doha rhyme) positions favour archaic trochaic long-penult endings metri causa (p. 9 n. 1); some ending pairs are heterogeneous (Prakrit loan vs native Apabhramsa) rather than prosodic variants (pp. 9-10); for polysyllabic nominal stems only the stem portion is concerned and prosody decides within it (p. 10).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent reconstructed for an extinct literary language from orthographic/metrical evidence (12th-c. Western Apabhramsa verse text); accent is never written and native grammarians are silent, so all statements are inferential and the classic authorities disagree.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog midd1350 'Late Middle Indo-Aryan' (alt. 'Middle Indo-Aryan', extinct, ref. Bubenik 2003) is the Apabhramsa stage of Indo-Aryan. Jacobi 1921 describes the (Western/Gurjara) Apabhramsa of Haribhadra's Neminahacariu (Gujarat, AD 1159) with counts from Dhanapala's Bhavisattakaha; Tagare 1948 covers Western, Southern and Eastern Apabhramsa 600-1200; Pischel 1900 sec. 46 speaks of 'poetic Apabhramsa' (Hemacandra, Pingala). Earlier Middle Indo-Aryan literary Prakrits have their own codes (maha1305 Maharastri, saur1252 Sauraseni, pali1273 Pali) and were checked separately; several files here are hard links to those downloads.

sources.note: Dedicated section: in Prakrit the place of the word accent was determined mechanically by the prosody (syllable quantity) of the word, as in Latin; for Apabhramsa Jacobi additionally posits an 'organic' accent on the stem (root) syllable (as in Gujarati) competing with the quantity accent, shown by preference for endings with short penult, shortening of -iuna/-isa after long root syllable, gemination of root-final consonants; enclitics throw their accent onto the final syllable of the preceding word (p. 8). Verified against page scan of p. 9 (p. 51).

sources.citation: Bloch, Jules. 1965. Indo-Aryan from the Vedas to Modern Times. English edition, largely revised by the author and translated by Alfred Master. Paris: Adrien-Maisonneuve (orig. L'indo-aryen du Veda aux temps modernes, 1934). p. 51.
sources.note: 'Middle Indian does not furnish any decisive facts in favour of a regular stress accent in the vulgar tongue.. The facts which have been adduced to prove a stress accent -- according to Pischel placed on the old tonic, and according to Jacobi on the first long vowel starting from the end of the word -- are open to other explanations, especially rhythm.'

sources.citation: Chatterji, Suniti Kumar. 1926. The Origin and Development of the Bengali Language, vol. 1. Calcutta: Calcutta University Press. pp. 276-278, 295, 312.
sources.note: Second-hand survey: Jacobi's Latin-like MIA stress (first long syllable from the end, secondary on first syllable) vs Pischel's two systems (poetic Apabhramsa among dialects keeping Vedic accent place) vs Turner vs Bloch's scepticism; 'absence of sure evidence.. leaves room only for a hypothesis'. Sec. 155 p. 312 assumes stress 'on non-initial syllables, in Apabhransa and in Old Bengali'; p. 295 initial phrase stress in East Magadhan Apabhransa/Old Bengali.
